```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(cosetsampling)
```

Coset designs select samples that are exactly balanced on several overlapping stratifications at once, when
the units of the frame are indexed by a vector space over a prime field and the stratifications are coset
partitions: margins and cross-classifications of a complete factorial frame, or rows, columns and wrapped
diagonals of a square grid of prime side. A coset design draws a random admissible direction and a random
set of cosets of it, so its first- and second-order inclusion probabilities, and the exact variance of the
sample mean, are available in closed form.

## A grid balanced on rows, columns and both wrapped diagonals

The data set `volcano` gives elevations on a grid; its rows 14 to 74 form a $61 \times 61$ block, and 61 is
prime. Unit $(i, j)$ is unit number $61 i + j + 1$ of the frame.

```{r}
g <- grid_frame(61)
y <- as.vector(t(volcano[14:74, ]))
S4 <- strata_grid(g, c("rows", "columns", "antidiagonals", "diagonals"))
main_effect_count(g, S4)
```

Lines in any of the $62 - 4 = 58$ other directions meet every row, column and diagonal exactly once. The
uniform mixture over these directions is an equal-weight design: it spreads the variance weight evenly over
the frequencies left free by balance, which makes it minimax over responses with bounded residual variance.

```{r}
d1 <- coset_design(g, S4, h = 1)          # samples of 61 units
d3 <- coset_design(g, S4, h = 1, r = 3)   # unions of 3 lines, 183 units
d1
is_equal_weight(d1)
design_effect(d1, y)
s <- draw_sample(d3)
balance_check(g, S4, s$units)$exact
```

With three cosets the random-group estimator is unbiased, and the regression estimator on the main-effects
model is more stable:

```{r}
random_group_variance(s, y, d3)$variance
regression_variance(s, y, g, S4)$variance
design_variance(d3, y)
```

Balancing on fewer stratifications gives the design effects of equal-weight designs for rows only, rows and
columns, and so on:

```{r}
fam <- c("rows", "columns", "antidiagonals", "diagonals")
sapply(1:4, function(j) design_effect(coset_design(g, strata_grid(g, fam[1:j]), h = 1), y))
```

## A complete factorial frame

A complete factorial with seven binary variables has $2^7 = 128$ units. With samples of four units balanced
on every variable there are 364 admissible directions, but no mixture of them is an equal-weight design; the
minimax mixture (which needs the package lpSolve) has a worst case 7.5% above the bound.

```{r}
f <- coset_frame(2, 7)
S <- strata_margins(f)
length(admissible_directions(f, S, h = 2))
uniform <- coset_design(f, S, h = 2)
worst_case_factor(uniform)
if (requireNamespace("lpSolve", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mm <- minimax_mixture(f, S, h = 2)
  mm$ratio
}
```

With eight units an equal-weight design exists, and so does one for the two-variable margins with 16 units.
For larger frames the directions can be drawn by rejection without listing them:

```{r}
S2 <- strata_margins(f, order = 2)
dr <- coset_design(f, S2, h = 4, nu = "rejection")
s <- draw_sample(dr)
balance_check(f, S2, s$units)$exact
```

`factorial_frame()` maps a data frame with one row per combination of categories to the frame.

## Placing other designs on the same scale

Samples from any design with inclusion probabilities $k/N$ can be evaluated by their main-effect weight share
$\tau$, which is zero exactly for exactly balanced designs, and by the lower bound on the worst-case variance
when main effects are bounded by $C$ times the residual variance. Here for simple random sampling, which has
$\tau = d_{\mathcal S}/(N - 1)$:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
srs <- replicate(2000, sample.int(g$N, 61), simplify = FALSE)
main_effect_share(g, S4, srs, k = 61)
worst_case_bound(g, S4, srs, k = 61, C = 1)
```

The same functions apply to samples from the cube method or other balancing algorithms.
